title: session-orchestration-thoughtbook
content:
Purpose:
Quick brainbook for an experimental "ordinal session lane" approach to session orchestration. This is intentionally informal — scribbles, tradeoffs, and minimal API sketches to help a 1:1 with SRE and a later whiteboard session.

Goals (non-exhaustive):
- Keep per-session latency SLOs while enabling multi-tenant batching + cache-sharing.
- Allow low-cost prefetching of KV prefixes without hard-reserving GPU capacity.
- Make session-control surface small and auditable for private deployments.
- Provide clear back-pressure signals so client SDKs can gracefully degrade.

High-level idea (one-liner):
Assign each live session an ordinal lane (0..N-1) that maps to soft execution priorities and prefetch budgets. The orchestration layer keeps a light-weight lease map for active ordinals and coordinates prefetch and batching windows.

Why ordinal lanes?
- Deterministic mapping avoids large per-session maps (just shard by hash -> ordinal).
- Ordinal conveys both affinity (which worker shard handles warm cache) and relative priority (lower ordinal -> higher prefetch budget).
- Lanes allow compact radios to express QoS: e.g. lane 0 = interactive with small-burst prefetches, lane 7 = background embeddings.

ASCII diagram:

                  +----------------+       +-----------------+
Client SDK ->    |  Ingress Layer  |  ->   |  Orchestration   |
 (http/gRPC)     +----------------+       +-----------------+
                                             |     |    |
                                             |     |    |
                                   +---------+     |    +--------+
                                   |               |             |
                                +-----+         +-----+       +-----+
                                |Pool0|         |Pool1|  ...  |PoolM|
                                +-----+         +-----+       +-----+
                                   |               |             |
                              +----------+     +----------+  +----------+
                              |Session DB|     |KV Cache  |  |Sidecar   |
                              |(leases)  |     |(prefetch)|  |prefetcher |
                              +----------+     +----------+  +----------+

Key runtime behaviors:
- On new session open, ingress returns a lane_id = hash(session_id) % L. It then posts a lightweight lease record to Session DB: {session_id, lane_id, epoch_ts, ephemeral_ver}.
- Orchestrator monitors leases (poll/push) and maintains local slot view to schedule prefetch windows for each lane.
- Pools are elastic. If pool serving lane K goes down, fallback routes to compatible lane (higher ordinal) with degraded prefetch budgets.
- Sidecar prefetcher runs near client (or co-located) to warm short prefix KV ranges (useful for deterministic system prompts).

Compact session-control API (HTTP minimal):
POST /v1/sessions
Headers: Authorization: Bearer <token>
Body: {"client_id":"cli-123","session_id":"s-987","desired_lane":null}
Response: {"session_id":"s-987","lane":3,"lease":"l-abc123","expires_at":"2025-02-25T18:42:00Z"}

PATCH /v1/sessions/{session_id}
Body: {"touch":true}  -> extends lease TTL
Body: {"desired_lane":5}  -> optimistic request; may be rejected with 409 if conflict

DELETE /v1/sessions/{session_id}  -> release lease immediately

Event hooks (webhook + ephemeral pubsub):
- on_lease_acquired(session_id, lane, ttl)
- on_lease_revoked(session_id, reason)
- on_lane_fallback(session_id, from_lane, to_lane, reason)

Prefetch model (budget semantics):
- Each lane has a per-minute token budget (prefetch_tokens_per_minute). Lower ordinal lanes have higher budgets. Budgets are consumed when sidecar or orchestrator issues prefetch requests.
- Prefetch results are cached in distributed KV with TTL and a "validation hash" to detect divergent system prompts.
- If prefetch cache miss on request path, runtime can either block (if lane is interactive) or issue async warm and serve degraded answers depending on client signal.

Config sketch (HCL-like) - minimal and intended for private-deploy config file:

orchestration {
  lanes = 8
  lane_defaults {
    prefetch_tokens_per_minute = 60
    lease_ttl_seconds = 60
  }

  lane_overrides = [
    { ordinal = 0, prefetch_tokens_per_minute = 300, lease_ttl_seconds = 120 },
    { ordinal = 6, prefetch_tokens_per_minute = 10 }
  ]

  session_db {
    endpoint = "https://session-db.internal"
    write_timeout_ms = 120
  }

  fallback_policy = "ordinal_recede" # try next higher ordinal up to N-1
}

Compact API shape (proto-like) for internal gRPC mapping:
message CreateSession { string client_id = 1; string session_id = 2; optional int32 desired_lane = 3; }
message CreateSessionResp { string session_id = 1; int32 lane = 2; string lease = 3; int64 expires_at_unix = 4; }

Operational notes / heuristics: 
- Choose L (num lanes) proportional to 1/2 * typical concurrent sessions per worker shard so hash skew doesn't cause overconcentration.
- Lease TTL should be small enough to allow quick reclamation on crash but long enough to avoid noisy churn (start ~60s).
- Offer a lightweight client-side backoff: on 503 or lane_fallback, client should try next best lane after randomized jitter.

Edge cases and tradeoffs:
- Large-tail clients: a single enterprise can have many sessions; ordinal hashing can split their sessions across lanes unintentionally. Consider an enterprise override (tenant affinity) that pins all their sessions to a small ordinal subset.
- Migration: rolling lane count change (L->L') needs migration strategy. Option A: re-hash on new sessions only, gradually drift. Option B: ephemeral mapping layer that mirrors old->new ordinals for a grace period.
- Security: leases are sensitive; sign lease tokens with HMAC using KMS key so private deployments can verify without contacting control plane for every request.

Open questions to resolve in sync w/ SRE and SDK leads:
- How much telemetry is affordable per-request for lease validation? (trace-level vs sampling)
- Should we expose lane hints in the hosted API or only as opaque lease tokens?
- Tradeoffs of client-side sidecar prefetcher vs orchestrator-driven prefetch (bandwidth and trust boundaries).
- Metrics: lane_hit_rate, prefetch_budget_consumption, lease_renewal_rate, lane_fallback_rate. Baselines?

Next steps / immediate actions:
- Pair with Jae to run a sim: synthetic 10k sessions, 8 lanes, run 24h to estimate prefetch budget hit/miss and tail latency impact. (owner: Jae)
- Draft a short RFC for lane migration semantics and lease token HMAC design (owner: Aisha).
- Quick SDK API shim prototype (JS/Python) that implements client-side graceful degradation (owner: Lina).

Random notes / scribbles:
- Consider combining lane ordinal with a micro-priority float derived from request metadata (e.g., interactive_flag + user_ttl).
- Might be useful to encode lane in JWT scopes for edge proxies to make local routing decisions without DB lookup.

References / comparables:
- Prefetch/batching ideas inspired by paper: "Efficient KV Caching for Transformer Serving" (internal reading notes)
- Look at past experiment: runtime/prefetch-experiment-2024 for budget heuristics (PR linked above)

If this resonates, schedule a 30m whiteboard with runtime + SDK + SRE. Bring: Jae, Lina, 1 SRE, 1 SDK engineer.

End of thoughtbook.
